props.title: Khartoum
props.initialSlug: Epic clash over Sudan's fate pits East vs. West

sections.content: Khartoum stands as one of the last great epic films of the 1960s, following the tradition of Lawrence of Arabia (1962) and Zulu (1964) in depicting colonial-era conflicts in Africa and the Middle East. Charlton Heston delivers a commanding performance as British General Charles "Chinese" Gordon, while Laurence Olivier's portrayal of the Mahdi, though controversial by modern standards, showcases the film's attempt to present both sides of the Anglo-Sudan conflict. The film's stunning 70mm Ultra Panavision cinematography captures the sweeping Sudanese landscapes and massive battle sequences with a grandeur rarely achieved in modern historical epics.

sections.content: The historical accuracy of Khartoum sets it apart from many colonial-era epics. Unlike The Four Feathers (1939) or Storm Over the Nile (1955), the film attempts to present a more nuanced view of imperialism and religious conflict. Director Basil Dearden and screenwriter Robert Ardrey extensively researched the 1884-85 Siege of Khartoum, resulting in dialogue that often quotes directly from Gordon's journals and historical documents. The film's treatment of the Mahdi's Islamic revolution shows remarkable depth for its era, though modern viewers might find some portrayals dated.

The film's influence can be seen in later historical epics like The Man Who Would Be King (1975) and Mountains of the Moon (1990), which similarly explore the complex relationship between European colonizers and indigenous peoples. The siege sequences influenced later films like Black Hawk Down (2001) and The Last Stand at Khartoum (2016), showing how military hubris and cultural misunderstanding can lead to devastating consequences. sections.content: Khartoum marks a transition point between classic colonial adventures like Sanders of the River (1935) and more critical examinations of imperialism such as Gandhi (1982). The film's production values - including massive practical effects and thousands of extras - represent the end of an era before CGI would transform how historical epics were made. Modern films like The Last King of Scotland (2006) and Beasts of No Nation (2015) take a much harder look at colonialism's legacy in Africa, making Khartoum an important historical document of changing attitudes.
